story.e: The boy Samuel was in the Lord’s service beside Eli. In those days the Lord spoke rarely, and visions were few. One night Eli, whose eyes had grown weak, lay down in his place, and Samuel lay down in the house of the Lord, where the holy ark was; the lamp had not yet gone out. Then the Lord called Samuel: “Samuel!” He answered: “Here I am!” — and ran to Eli: “Did you call me?” Eli said: “I did not call you, my son; go back and lie down.” It happened a second time too: the Lord called, and Samuel ran to Eli. Eli sent him back again. Samuel did not yet know the Lord and did not know that it was his word calling. The Lord called a third time, and when Samuel ran over again, Eli understood what was happening. He said to him: “Go, lie down, and if he calls again, answer like this: Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening!” Samuel went back and lay down. Then the Lord came, stood beside him, and called as before: “Samuel, Samuel!” And he answered: “Speak, for your servant is listening!” The Lord then gave a hard message about Eli’s house: he would no longer overlook the abuses, because Eli knew of them and did not intervene. Samuel lay there until morning and was afraid to tell Eli the vision. But Eli called him: “My son, what did he say to you? Hide nothing from me!” Then Samuel told him everything. Eli answered: “It is the Lord; let him do what seems right to him.” Samuel grew up, and the Lord was with him: not one of his words fell to the ground. All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, learned that the Lord had made Samuel his prophet, and the Lord continued to appear to him at Shiloh through his word.
story.m: The boy Samuel was in the Lord’s service beside Eli. In those days the Lord spoke rarely, and visions were few in Israel. One night it happened that Eli, whose eyes had grown so weak that he could barely see, lay down in his place, while Samuel lay down in the house of the Lord, where God’s holy ark was; God’s lamp had not yet gone out. Then the Lord called Samuel, and he answered: “Here I am!” He ran to Eli and said: “Here I am; you called me.” Eli answered: “I did not call you, my son; go back and lie down!” Samuel went back and lay down. The Lord called a second time: “Samuel!” He got up, went to Eli and said: “Here I am; you called me.” Eli answered: “I did not call you, my son; go back and lie down!” At that time Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the Lord had not yet revealed his word to him. The Lord called Samuel a third time, and he got up, went to Eli and said: “Here I am; you called me.” Then Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy, and he said to him: “Go, lie down, and if he calls, answer like this: Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening!” Samuel went and lay down in his place. Then the Lord came, stood beside him and called as on the earlier occasions: “Samuel, Samuel!” And he answered: “Speak, for your servant is listening!” The Lord said to Samuel: “I am about to do such a thing in Israel that the ears of everyone who hears it will ring. On that day I will fulfil against Eli’s house everything I declared about it. I made known to him that I would judge his house for their guilt, because he knew his sons were sinning gravely and did not stop them.” Samuel lay there until morning, then opened the doors of the house of the Lord. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision. But Eli called him: “Samuel, my son!” He answered: “Here I am.” Eli asked: “What is it he said to you? Please hide nothing from me! May God deal with you as he sees fit if you keep back anything of what he said to you.” Then Samuel told him everything and hid nothing. And Eli answered: “It is the Lord: let him do what seems right to him!” Samuel grew up, and the Lord was with him: he did not let a single one of his words fall to the ground. All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, learned that the Lord had made Samuel his prophet. The Lord continued to appear at Shiloh, for there he revealed himself to Samuel through his word; and Samuel passed on the Lord’s word to all Israel.
story.h: This chapter is the last piece of module three, and it is here for a reason: the age of the judges closed with “everyone did as they saw fit”, and this chapter is precisely about how God’s word speaks again in a world that had stopped expecting it. Four things are worth seeing apart. The first is the opening sentence: “in those days the Lord spoke rarely, and visions were few.” That is not a passing remark but a description of a condition. The sanctuary is working, the priests are in place, the rites go on — and still there is silence. The Bible says here that a religious institution can keep running after the living relationship has ended. The second is the series of misunderstandings. Samuel runs to Eli three times, and it is not the child’s fault: “Samuel did not yet know the Lord.” The text describes very humanly that a calling cannot be recognised automatically, and that someone is needed to teach it. And here is Eli’s role, the chapter’s greatest turn: Eli is a bad priest and a failed father, yet at the decisive moment he teaches rightly. He tells the boy what to answer. The news of the judgement, in other words, is brought home by the man against whom the judgement is spoken. The Bible thereby allows someone to be a failure and still useful — a very grown-up idea. The third is the form of the answer: “Speak, for your servant is listening.” Notice that Samuel asks no question and offers nothing: he undertakes to listen. In the age of the judges everyone acted by their own measure; here someone says that first he will listen. That is the module’s real closing chord. The fourth is Samuel’s first task, which is very hard: the first thing he receives from God is a message he is afraid to deliver — and he delivers it. He becomes a prophet not because he received visions but because what he received he did not keep back, not even when it concerned his own teacher. The chapter’s end sums this up exactly: “he did not let a single one of his words fall to the ground.” From here Israel’s next section begins: Samuel will be the one to anoint the first king, and later David as well. Module three, then, travels from the entry into the land, through the collapse of the judges, to a boy who says in the middle of the night: I am listening.

verse.text: Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening!

bio.hu: Mózes után ő vezette a népet az ígéret földjére. Isten azt mondta neki: légy erős és bátor, mert veled vagyok, ahova csak mész. Nem a saját erejében bízott: Jerikó falai nem a hadsereg miatt omlottak le.
bio.en: After Moses he led the people into the promised land. God said to him: be strong and courageous, for I am with you wherever you go. He did not trust his own strength: the walls of Jericho did not fall because of an army.

hu.q: Ki után vezette Józsué a népet?

en.q: Whom did Joshua follow as leader?

hu.q: Mit mondott Isten Józsuénak az elhívásánál?
o: Légy erős és bátor, veled vagyok

en.q: What did God say to Joshua when he called him?
o: Be strong and courageous, I am with you

hu.q: Melyik folyón kelt át a nép Józsuéval?

en.q: Which river did the people cross with Joshua?

hu.q: Mit állítottak fel a folyó közepéről vett kövekből?

en.q: What did they set up from the stones taken from the riverbed?
What happened to the walls of Jericho?

hu.q: Hányszor kerülték meg a várost az utolsó napon?

en.q: How many times did they march round the city on the last day?

o: Hogy ki lesz a következő vezető

en.q: What did Joshua ask in his farewell speech?
o: Who the next leader would be
How much land they would get

hu.q: Mit felelt Józsué a saját kérdésére?
o: Én és az én házam az Urat szolgáljuk

en.q: How did Joshua answer his own question?
o: As for me and my household, we will serve the LORD

hu.q: Mit tanít Józsué története a bátorságról?
o: Nem a félelem hiánya, hanem Isten jelenléte adja
Aki bátor, az nem fél soha

en.q: What does Joshua's story teach about courage?
o: It comes from God's presence, not from the absence of fear
Courage is something we are born with

bio.hu: Jerikói nő, aki elrejtette a két kémet a háza tetején. Nem a népéhez tartozott, és nem is volt feddhetetlen élete, mégis ő hitte el, hogy Isten adja a földet Izráelnek. A piros zsinór az ablakában megmentette a családját — és a Máté evangéliumának első fejezetében ott van a neve Jézus nemzetségtáblájában.
bio.en: A woman of Jericho who hid the two spies on her roof. She did not belong to Israel, and her life had not been blameless, yet she believed that God was giving the land to Israel. The scarlet cord in her window saved her family — and her name appears in Jesus' family line in the first chapter of Matthew.

en.q: In which city did Rahab live?
Whom did Rahab hide?

o: A háza tetején, a lenkóró alatt

en.q: Where did she hide them?
o: On her roof, under the flax

en.q: What did Rahab ask of the spies?

hu.q: Mi volt a jel az ablakában?

en.q: What was the sign in her window?

hu.q: Mit mondott Ráháb Istenről a kémeknek?
o: Hogy tudja: Isten nekik adja ezt a földet

en.q: What did Rahab say about God to the spies?
o: That she knew God was giving them this land
That her own gods were stronger

en.q: What happened to Rahab's family?

hu.q: Hol szerepel még Ráháb neve az Újszövetségben?

en.q: Where else does Rahab's name appear in the New Testament?
o: In the address of Paul's letters
Isten azt is befogadja, aki kívülről jön
Csak a jó családból származók számítanak
Csak a saját népét szereti Isten

en.q: What does Rahab's story teach?
o: Only those from good families matter
The past determines everything for ever
God loves only his own people

bio.hu: Bíró és prófétanő, aki egy pálmafa alatt ült, és odajárt hozzá a nép igazságért. Amikor Bárák nem akart egyedül menni a csatába, ő vele ment. A győzelem után éneket szerzett, amely a Biblia egyik legősibb költeménye.
bio.en: A judge and prophetess who sat under a palm tree, and the people came to her for justice. When Barak would not go into battle alone, she went with him. After the victory she composed a song that is one of the oldest poems in the Bible.

en.q: What was Deborah's role?
o: She was a judge and prophetess

hu.q: Hol ült Debóra, amikor a nép hozzá jött?

en.q: Where did Deborah sit when the people came to her?

hu.q: Kit hívott el Debóra a csatába?

en.q: Whom did Deborah summon to battle?
What did Barak ask of Deborah?
What did Deborah answer?
What happened after the battle?
What is special about Deborah's song?
o: It is one of the oldest poems in the Bible
It is only one line long
God's name does not appear in it

hu.q: Mit mutat Debóra története a vezetésről?
o: Isten azt hív el, akit akar

en.q: What does Deborah's story show about leadership?

bio.hu: Amikor Isten elhívta, éppen a présházban rejtőzött a félelem miatt — és az angyal mégis így szólította: erős vitéz. Kétszer kért jelet a gyapjúval, mert félt. Isten pedig a seregét harminckétezerről háromszáz emberre csökkentette, hogy kiderüljön, kinek a győzelme ez.
bio.en: When God called him he was hiding in the winepress out of fear — and yet the angel greeted him: mighty warrior. He twice asked for a sign with the fleece, because he was afraid. And God cut his army from thirty-two thousand down to three hundred, so that it would be clear whose victory it was.

hu.q: Hol rejtőzött Gedeon, amikor Isten elhívta?

en.q: Where was Gideon hiding when God called him?
How did the angel greet him?

o: A gyapjú hol legyen nedves, hol száraz

en.q: What sign did Gideon ask for?
o: That the fleece be wet, then dry

en.q: How many times did he ask for the sign?
How many men did he start with?
How many were left in the end?

o: Hogy kiderüljön, kinek a győzelme ez

en.q: Why did God reduce the army?
o: So it would be clear whose victory it was

hu.q: Mi volt a háromszáz ember kezében?

en.q: What did the three hundred carry?
o: A trumpet and a torch inside a jar

hu.q: Mit tanít Gedeon története a félelemről?
o: Istennek nem a félelmetlenségünk kell, hanem az igenünk

en.q: What does Gideon's story teach about fear?
o: God does not need our fearlessness, only our yes

bio.hu: Születése előtt elhívta őt Isten, és rendkívüli erőt kapott. De az erejét sokszor magára használta, és a végén elárulta a titkát. A története nem sikertörténet: megvakítva, fogságban mondja ki az egyetlen igazi imádságát — és Isten akkor is meghallgatja.
bio.en: God called him before he was born and gave him extraordinary strength. But he often used that strength for himself, and in the end he gave away his secret. His story is not a success story: blinded and in prison he prays his one real prayer — and even then God hears him.

en.q: What did Samson receive from God?
When did God call Samson?
What was his secret?
To whom did he reveal his secret?

hu.q: Mi történt vele, amikor elvágták a haját?
o: Elhagyta az ereje, és fogságba került

en.q: What happened when his hair was cut?
o: His strength left him and he was taken captive

en.q: What did the Philistines do to him?
o: They blinded him and made him work
Hogy Isten emlékezzen rá még egyszer

en.q: What did Samson ask at the end?
o: That God remember him once more
That his hair be given back
Mert az erejét sokszor magára használta

en.q: Why is Samson's life not a success story?
o: Because he often used his strength for himself
Az ajándék nem helyettesíti a jellemet
A tehetség elég a jó élethez

en.q: What does Samson's story teach?
o: A gift is no substitute for character
Talent is enough for a good life

bio.hu: Moábi nő, aki az özvegy anyósával, Naómival maradt, amikor elmehetett volna haza. Ezt mondta neki: ahova te mész, oda megyek, és a te Istened az én Istenem. Idegenként gyűjtötte a kalászokat Boáz földjén, és végül ő lett Dávid király ősanyja.
bio.en: A Moabite woman who stayed with her widowed mother-in-law Naomi when she could have gone home. She said to her: where you go I will go, and your God will be my God. As a foreigner she gathered grain in Boaz's field, and in the end she became the great-grandmother of King David.

en.q: From which people did Ruth come?
With whom did Ruth stay?
What did Ruth say to Naomi?
o: Where you go I will go
I am going home to my people
A te Istened az én Istenem

en.q: What did Ruth say about Naomi's God?
o: Your God will be my God
I do not believe in him

en.q: What did Ruth do in Boaz's field?

hu.q: Miért szedhette össze a hátramaradt kalászokat?
o: Mert a törvény a szegényeknek és a jövevényeknek hagyta

en.q: Why was she allowed to gather the leftover grain?
o: Because the law left it for the poor and the foreigner

en.q: Who became Ruth's husband?
Whose ancestor did Ruth become?

o: A hűség és a jövevény befogadása Isten történetének része
Csak a saját néphez tartozók számítanak

en.q: What does Ruth's story teach?
o: Loyalty and welcoming the stranger belong to God's story
